meta.title: A Class Apart
meta.skill_frame: Find the main idea: decide what a whole passage is mostly about, not one true detail.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fifth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured FK 5.3 on the three parts together, inside the grade 4-5 band. The load is three facts about a group that only add up to a whole picture.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.basis: Adapted from the National Park Service, 'Canallers - Captains of the Canal', Chesapeake & Ohio Canal National Historical Park.
source.attribution: U.S. National Park Service, 'Canallers - Captains of the Canal', Chesapeake & Ohio Canal National Historical Park, https://www.nps.gov/choh/learn/historyculture/canallers.htm, accessed 2026-11-15. U.S. federal government work; public domain in the U.S.
source.text_status: Adapted, reading load reduced by splitting long sentences and cutting asides.
source.survey: The boatmen worked hard for little pay, kept to themselves, and made a life the towns along the canal never joined.
source.avoided: No invented wages; no detail about individual boatmen.

session.difficulty_basis: How far the stated idea sits from the words the passage uses.

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: Canallers were also called boatmen. They worked on the canal. Their work meant hard work, long hours, and little pay. The work had daring adventure. It also kept them apart from much of the world outside the canal. This adventure and isolation helped make the independent-minded boatmen a rough and ready group. They usually formed a class apart from their neighbors in the Potomac Valley. They often married within their own group. Their children were often born and raised in the trade. These children generally had little exposure to schooling or social polish from the growing American culture of the 1800s.
passage.part_2: The boatmen were constantly brawling among themselves. They fought with each other for first place at the locks. They also fought because of some real or imagined insult. Their life was at best irregular and unpredictable. It was not regular. It was not predictable. Some moved slowly along the line. Some amused themselves in drunken fun. They took their time in making the run. Others were more ambitious. They drove their teams and boats at full speed night and day. These ambitious boatmen cared little for themselves. They cared little for their mules or boats. They cared little for canal property.
passage.part_3: The boatmen were constantly at odds with the company. They did not agree with the company about toll rates and freight charges. They were also at odds with lock keepers. They did not agree with lock keepers about operating procedures or personal slights. Usually, the canallers shunned the larger towns along the canal. It cost too much to feed their teams. They also felt out of place in those larger towns. Even while wintering along the line, they had their own settlements. These settlements were on the fringes of the towns. They were often quite far away from the towns.
